cards.title: GA4 data retention: switch from 2 months to 14 months
cards.summary: Choose a suitable retention window for ecommerce explorations; standard aggregated reports are unaffected.
cards.use_when: Setting up a fresh GA4 property or auditing an existing one before relying on it for year-over-year ecommerce reporting.
steps: Open the correct GA4 property and review its Data Retention settings.
Where available and appropriate for the store, select 14 months for seasonal explorations. Verify property eligibility and required retention policy.
An increase preserves previously collected data that still exists; it cannot restore already deleted data.
caveats: Retention affects explorations and funnel reports, not standard aggregated reports. Large-property limits and some data categories have separate rules.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Prevent fragmented sessions by extending GA4 session timeout
cards.summary: GA4's default 30-minute session timeout can split a single shopping journey into multiple sessions, distorting engagement and conversion metrics.
cards.use_when: Configuring a new GA4 property or investigating why session counts and conversion rates look inflated or fragmented for a store with long browse-to-purchase lag.
steps: Open GA4 Admin > Data Streams > select the stream > Configure Tag Settings (or the data stream's session settings depending on current UI).
Locate the session timeout setting, which defaults to 30 minutes.
Increase it toward the allowed maximum (the source cites up to 7 hours and 55 minutes) when customers commonly leave and return within a browsing session on the same device.
Weigh the tradeoff: a longer timeout keeps a single journey intact but can merge genuinely separate visits into one session, lowering apparent per-session conversion rate.
Re-check the resulting session and conversion-rate reports after the change to confirm the shift matches the store's real buying behavior.
caveats: Choosing the maximum is not automatically correct; the source presents extending the timeout as a fix for fragmented sessions, not a universal requirement. Test against the store's actual purchase lag.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Configure cross-domain tracking for checkout on a separate domain
cards.summary: If any step of a purchase journey crosses domains (e.g., a third-party checkout), analytics without cross-domain tracking will attribute the sale to a new session and lose the true source.
cards.use_when: Setting up analytics for a store whose checkout, cart, or landing flow uses a different domain than the main site — common with hosted checkouts and upsell tools.
steps: Map the full customer journey and list every domain a single visitor touches between landing and purchase.
Decide whether to use one GA4 property spanning all of them; the source recommends a single property with cross-domain tracking when visitors jump between domains in one journey.
In GA4 Admin, open the data stream's Configure Tag Settings and add the additional domains under 'Configure your domains'.
Verify by running through a full purchase journey and confirming it appears as one session with the original acquisition source intact, not as a referral from your own checkout domain.
Also exclude internal/office IP traffic so staff testing the checkout don't pollute conversion data.
caveats: Cross-domain tracking around third-party checkout systems can be limited by how that vendor handles redirects and iframes; confirm compatibility with the checkout provider. Verify current GA4 cross-domain setup steps in the interface.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Filter internal office IP traffic out of GA4
cards.summary: Office and testing traffic inflates sessions and distorts conversion metrics, so define and exclude it during setup.
cards.use_when: New GA4 setup or ongoing data-quality audit for a store where staff frequently visit the site to test products, pricing, or checkout.
steps: Find the public IP address(es) of the office or any location where staff browse and test the store.
In GA4 Admin > Data Streams > Configure Tag Settings > Define Internal Traffic, add a rule matching those IP addresses.
Create or activate an 'Internal Traffic' exclusion filter (data filter) at the property level, using the internal-traffic rule and setting it to exclude.
Confirm the filter is active rather than in testing mode before relying on the data.
Re-test with a request from the office network and confirm it does not appear in real-time reports.
caveats: Home-office and VPN traffic uses changing IPs and is not fully filtered by this method. GA4 filters can take effect going forward only and may not restate past data.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Create custom GA4 events via GTM with triggers and parameters
cards.summary: Track meaningful on-page interactions (like menu link clicks) as custom GA4 events by configuring them in Google Tag Manager with precise triggers and parameters.
cards.use_when: Building out analytics for a store where default GA4 events don't capture the interactions that matter for merchandising or navigation decisions.
steps: In GTM, create a new Tag using the 'GA4 Event' tag type and give the event a name using only lowercase letters and underscores (GA4 naming convention) — e.g., menu_link_click.
Create a Trigger for the interaction, using conditions such as 'Click Classes' contains a specific class or 'Click Element' matching a selector, so the trigger fires only on the intended clicks.
Map custom parameters in the tag — for example menu_item_name and menu_item_url — using GTM variables to pull the clicked item's text or href.
Use GTM Preview mode to connect to the site, trigger the interaction, and confirm the tag fired.
Use GA4 DebugView to confirm the event and its parameters were actually received by GA4 before publishing the container.
caveats: Custom parameters will not appear in GA4 standard reports until you register them as Custom Dimensions in the GA4 admin panel and data finishes processing.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Register GTM custom parameters as GA4 Custom Dimensions
cards.summary: Custom event parameters you send through GTM are invisible in GA4 reports until you register them as Custom Dimensions.
cards.use_when: After setting up a custom event (e.g., menu link clicks) and finding its parameters are not available for reporting or explorations.
steps: Confirm the parameter is already being sent, verified via DebugView.
In GA4 Admin > Custom Definitions > Custom Dimensions, create a new dimension.
Set the Dimension Name (a friendly label for reports) and the Event Parameter (the exact parameter key sent in the tag, e.g., menu_item_name), matching case exactly.
Choose the correct scope (Event scope for event parameters).
Allow 24 to 48 hours for GA4 to process the data before the dimension appears populated in standard reports.
caveats: GA4 processing lag means newly registered dimensions won't show data immediately; don't assume the setup failed. Also, GTM preview and DebugView are more reliable for verifying parameters than standard reports right after configuration.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Test GA4/GTM event setup before publishing the container
cards.summary: Verify every new tracking tag in GTM Preview and GA4 DebugView before publishing, so broken tracking doesn't silently corrupt data.
cards.use_when: Any time you add or change a tracking tag for a store, before pushing the change live to all users.
steps: Open GTM Preview mode and connect to the site.
Perform the real interaction you want to track (click, add-to-cart, etc.).
In GTM Preview, confirm the correct trigger fired and the tag executed.
Open GA4 DebugView (via Admin > DebugView, or with the Stream URL) and confirm the event name and all parameters arrived with the correct values.
Only after both GTM and DebugView confirm success, publish the GTM container version.
Allow 24 to 48 hours for GA4 to process event data before expecting it in standard reports.
caveats: The source warns GA4 takes 24 to 48 hours to fully process events, so new tags won't appear in reports instantly. DebugView is temporary and only shows a recent window of debug events.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Use a single GA4 property across domains in one journey
cards.summary: When a single customer journey crosses multiple domains, the source recommends one GA4 property with cross-domain tracking rather than separate properties.
cards.use_when: Deciding property architecture for a store that uses a main site plus a separate checkout, landing, or app domain.
steps: Trace the visitor journey and identify all domains involved.
If visitors jump between domains within a single purchase journey, configure one single GA4 property rather than splitting them.
Enable cross-domain tracking in the data stream by listing all involved domains under 'Configure your domains'.
Test a full journey to confirm it resolves to a single session with the original source, not self-referrals.
Keep the acquisition and monetization data unified so attribution and conversion counts stay accurate.
caveats: This is the source's recommendation for multi-domain journeys; a single-property setup can complicate administration if the domains serve genuinely separate businesses with different owners or reporting needs.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Reverse-engineer the purchase path with Path Exploration
cards.summary: GA4 Path Exploration lets you start from a purchase event and work backward to see the sequence of pages and events preceding conversions.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing where buyers drop off or what pages precede a purchase, to inform merchandising and PDP/checkout improvements.
steps: Open GA4 Explore and create a Path Exploration.
Set the end-point (or starting-point) node to the Purchase event and work backward to see the common preceding steps.
Alternatively, start from a high-traffic landing page and forward-track where users go next.
Identify the most common paths to purchase and the points where users exit or stall — these are friction candidates.
Translate the top friction points into testable changes (e.g., PDP layout, add-to-cart placement, cart-step clarity) rather than guessing.
caveats: Explorations are subject to sampling and data thresholds, and require enough traffic volume to be reliable. Path exploration reflects correlation of sequences, not proof of causation.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Build Free Form tables in GA4 Explorations
cards.summary: Free Form analysis in GA4 lets you build custom cross-tabulated tables of dimensions and metrics to answer specific store questions beyond standard reports.
cards.use_when: When a store question (e.g., which products convert best by traffic source, or how a specific landing page performs) is not answerable from GA4's standard reports.
steps: Open GA4 Explore and create a Blank or Free Form exploration.
Drag in Dimensions (e.g., landing page, session source/medium, device category) as rows or columns.
Add Metrics (e.g., sessions, conversions, revenue, engagement rate) as values.
Apply filters or segments to isolate the question, such as a single campaign or product category.
Interpret with caution due to data thresholds and sampling on smaller segments, and export or screenshot before the exploration expires.
caveats: Explorations are not saved indefinitely the way standard reports are; heavier filtering increases sampling and thresholding, which can hide data on low-traffic segments.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Extend the engaged-session threshold above the 10-second default
cards.summary: GA4's default engaged-session threshold of 10 seconds understates meaningful engagement, so the source recommends raising it to at least 30 seconds.
cards.use_when: Configuring GA4 settings for a store where you want engagement metrics to reflect genuine browsing rather than momentary visits.
steps: Locate the engaged-session definitions in GA4 configuration (Admin > Data Streams > Configure Tag Settings or session settings depending on current UI).
Note that GA4's default treats a session as engaged at 10 seconds.
Adjust the threshold to at least 30 seconds per the source's recommendation.
Revisit engagement-rate reporting to confirm it now better reflects real browsing behavior rather than brief visits.
Use the adjusted metric when comparing landing pages or traffic sources for engagement quality.
caveats: The 30-second figure is the source's recommendation, not an industry standard; choose a threshold matching your product's consideration time. Changing definitions affects comparability with historical data.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Enable Google Signals for demographic audience data
cards.summary: Google Signals provides demographic reporting (age, gender, interests) and enables cross-device information in GA4.
cards.use_when: When you want demographic or interest data to guide ad targeting, creative strategy, or audience definitions for a store.
steps: In GA4 Admin > Data Settings > Data Collection, enable Google Signals under Data Collection and Modification.
Review what has changed in current GA4 versions — the data collection toggle and privacy controls have shifted over time, so verify the current interface.
Once enabled and after data accumulates, review demographic reports to understand the age/gender/interest composition of converting vs. non-converting segments.
Apply insights to ad audience selection and creative strategy rather than to individual-level targeting decisions.
Confirm consent/privacy compliance for your regions before enabling, since Signals uses Google's signed-in user data.
caveats: Enabling Google Signals requires a privacy/compliance review; it involves Google-signed-in user data and can be restricted in some jurisdictions. The source lists it as one of five mandatory settings but also the availability and behavior can vary by region.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Apply GA4 naming conventions to custom events
cards.summary: Use lowercase letters and underscores for GA4 event names to keep tracking consistent and avoid downstream reporting breaks.
cards.use_when: Creating any custom event in GA4/GTM for a store, or standardizing event names across teams and tools.
steps: When naming a custom event, restrict it to lowercase letters and underscores — e.g., cart_add_item, menu_link_click.
Avoid spaces, camelCase, or mixed case in event names, which the source warns against for GA4.
Keep naming consistent across tags so reports aggregate properly rather than splitting the same action across variants.
Document event names so future team members use the same conventions.
Note that GA4 has reserved/automatic event names; avoid colliding with them.
caveats: The source specifically states the lowercase-and-underscore requirement for GA4 event names; verify against current GA4 documentation since accepted conventions can evolve.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Treat GA4 setup as a five-setting baseline for ecommerce accuracy
cards.summary: The source identifies five mandatory GA4 admin configurations to make ecommerce data trustworthy before you rely on it.
cards.use_when: Onboarding a new GA4 property or auditing an established store analytics setup before making merchandising or marketing decisions from it.
steps: 1) Extend data retention from the 2-month default to 14 months.
2) Configure cross-domain tracking if the journey spans domains.
3) Define and filter internal office/office IP traffic.
4) Extend the default 30-minute session timeout toward the allowed maximum to avoid fragmented sessions.
5) Enable Google Signals for demographic data (subject to privacy review).
Verify each setting is active and not just staged, then re-test a purchase journey end-to-end before trusting the numbers.
caveats: These are the source's prescribed baseline settings, some of which (maximum session timeout, Signals) carry tradeoffs or compliance considerations. Treat them as a starting checklist, not universal rules; verify current GA4 interface behavior.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 tutorial for beginners (2026) __ GA4 tutorial for beginners __ GA4 course.docx

cards.title: Do not rely on AI chat assistants for GA4 technical configuration
cards.summary: The source warns that an AI analytics chat assistant hallucinated incorrect technical advice about GA4, so verify AI-generated setup guidance against GA4's actual interface.
cards.use_when: When seeking quick answers on GA4 setup or landing-page attribution issues, before applying AI-generated configuration advice to a live store property.
steps: Treat AI-suggested GA4 configuration steps as hypotheses, not instructions.
Verify any claim (e.g., how 'not set' landing pages work) against GA4's official documentation or the interface itself.
Where AI advice conflicts with observed DebugView/Preview behavior, trust the observed data.
Keep a record of what actually works in your property for future reference.
Avoid applying AI-suggested changes to a production container without the GTM Preview/DebugView verification step.
caveats: This reflects the source's experience with a specific AI assistant; it's a caution about verification, not a claim that all AI tools are useless.
